newsitem.title: LUXEMBOURG: Little progress on EU reforms, extra summit looms.
newsitem.headline: Little progress on EU reforms, extra summit looms.

text.p: Just six weeks before EU leaders are due to sign landmark treaty reforms at a summit in Amsterdam, the bloc's foreign ministers remained bogged down on Tuesday in the nuts and bolts of institutional changes.

Meeting to continue preparations for the summit on the inter-governmental conference (IGC), ministers remained divided over the size of a future European Commission, the EU's executive arm, and how to ensure that the decision-making process fairly represents each country's population.

"A lot of matters have become clearer, but I won't hide from you that the margin of manoeuvre for national governments is limited...," Dutch Foreign Minister and EU president Hans van Mierlo told reporters.

"It's becoming clearer that it is difficult to achieve consensus (among foreign ministers) and it is highly likely that these issues can only be sorted out when heads of governments get to grips with them."

With national elections in both Britain and France hampering progress on the IGC, the Dutch are resigned to calling a special informal summit in late May, but Van Mierlo said no firm decision had yet been taken on this.

He did, however, give a strong hint that, if an extra meeting of heads of state and government were called, it would take place in the Dutch coastal resort of Noordwijk and not in Maastricht as widely expected. The likely date remains May 23.
An extra summit would give member states the chance to quiz a likely new British Labour government on its stance towards deeper EU integration as planned under the IGC.
Britain's ruling Conservatives, trailing badly in polls one day ahead of the election, are seen as more sceptical towards Europe than their Labour rivals.
"We will be asking for a major effort from a new British government (to get up-to-speed on the IGC)," van Mierlo said.

The IGC, a ministerial review of the EU's "constitution", aims to produce a more efficient and transparent Union, paving the way for an ambitious eastward expansion that could see up to a dozen ex-communist states joining in the next decade.
Ministers earlier discussed a well-backed Franco-German plan to fully integrate the Western European Union (WEU) defence agency into the EU, but Britain remained opposed to this.
Van Mierlo said there were differences on a target date for completing WEU integration and over how joint security actions should be funded.

The smaller EU states, keen to preserve their seats on the Commission, are reluctant to agree to a major slimming down of the 20-seat executive and latest proposals suggest a future body of 15-20 Commissioners with fewer portfolios and more power for the Commission president.
